extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patentees, and patent practitioners (historical/common‑law context)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for drafting the specification part of a patent: what must be described, how the specification must relate to the patent, and what defects will render a patent void under common‑law authorities. Geared to ensuring sufficiency, accuracy, and proper scope of patent disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must be accurately ascertained and particularly described
rubrics_metrics.description: In the specification the invention must be accurately ascertained, and particularly described; it must be set forth in the most minute detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosure of the secret is the price of the monopoly; the specification ought to be full and correct so that the subject of the patent may be well known at expiration and the public may reap the same advantages. If the specification is materially false or defective the patent is void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement for a person of ordinary skill (mechanic of common understanding)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must be such that mechanical men of common understanding can comprehend it to make a machine by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It must allow mechanics to make the machine by following the directions without any new inventions or additions of their own. Sufficient disclosure exists if a person of moderate capacity with a little knowledge of the science can immediately see the method and apprehend the purport without study, invention of his own, or experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must disclose the secret as ample as patentee uses it
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must put the public in possession of the secret in as ample and beneficial a way as the patentee himself uses it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purpose of the specification is to teach the public what the art is after the patent term; inadequate disclosure defeats the consideration for the grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent and specification must support and explain one another
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent and the specification are connected and dependent on each other for support; each may be referred to in order to understand the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Still, the specification must itself contain a full description; taken together the patent and specification should be complete and afford every required information. The title in the patent links to the description in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must support the title of the patent (no incongruity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must support the title of the patent; the latter should not indicate one thing and the former describe another as the subject of the grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the petitioner represented himself as inventor of matter not truly claimed in the specification, the grant may be void. Example: a patent for a tapering brush was not supported by a specification describing bristles of unequal length (not actually tapering).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim more than the actual invention (no over‑claiming)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must not attempt to cover more than that which is the proper subject for protection; if a patentee seeks by his specification any more than he is strictly entitled to, his patent is rendered ineffectual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims exceeding the inventor's true discovery may invalidate the entire grant. Example: a patent for a machine plus an improvement where the machine part could not be sustained made the whole grant invalid for attempting to cover too much.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title should be commensurate: not too broad nor too narrow
rubrics_metrics.description: The title of the patent being a short description should not be very extensive nor very confined, but commensurate with the thing invented and correctly inform the public of its exact nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A title indicating, e.g., an improvement in lighting 'cities, towns, and villages' when the invention was a new lamp was considered too extensive and void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct choice of subject: substance vs. process vs. machine
rubrics_metrics.description: When the effect is some new substance or composition, the patent ought to be taken out for the new substance or composition; when the thing discovered is the means of producing one (a machine), the patent can only be maintained for the mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a new substance is really produced, the grant may be valid even if achieved by a process. Conversely, if only a process/mode is new but not a new substance, treating it as a patent for a substance may be inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification of a substance must describe materials, making method, and use
rubrics_metrics.description: In the specification of a substance the thing itself should be accurately ascertained: the materials of which it is composed, the method by which it is made, and the use to which it is to be applied should be accurately developed and particularly described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporeal substances rarely afford information of the mode of making or manner of using, so the specification must supply those details to make the invention intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description confined to the manufacture; avoid extraneous matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must be confined to the manufacture so that the novelty may be known; extraneous matter, however learned, must not be introduced to darken it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification need not teach complete novices, nor be so concise as to be obscure. Address the public generally but assume a modest baseline of knowledge in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous terms; explain technical or trade meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: If the terms in which the subject is expressed are ambiguous or used in a sense other than their ordinary meaning, the invention may be concealed and the grant invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a word has a technical meaning differing from common usage, it should be explained. Examples: 'white lead' used where effect only produced a similar substance; 'malt' meaning differently than common acceptance—should be clarified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not omit necessary descriptions (new parts must be clearly elucidated)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a specification all that is new must be clearly elucidated; the old parts need only be distinguished as material or immaterial in producing the desired effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material parts—even if well known—when applied in a new manner must be described. Omission of a material alteration (e.g., in rollers) or of parts used only for particular articles (e.g., Arkwright's hammer for flax) may be fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish old parts from new; avoid appearing to appropriate old matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must not appear to appropriate to himself any part which is old or has been used in other manufactures; old and immaterial parts should be named only as old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to mark known parts as old or treating them as essential may give the construction that the patentee seeks to monopolize more than he invented. Safest practice: describe entire subject and point out which parts are old.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insertion of useless or unnecessary parts (to mislead) invalidates the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: If things useless and unnecessary have been mixed with a substance or attached to a machine, even though terms are intelligible and necessary description present, the patent is void — such parts are presumed to have been introduced to mislead and conceal the real invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parts were never used by the patentee or are not necessary to produce the desired effect, their inclusion raises a presumption of deception. Occasional historical use does not remove suspicion unless there is a good reason for discontinuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: If specification lists multiple ways/ingredients and one fails, patent may be defective
rubrics_metrics.description: Where different ways or different ingredients are named and one of them fails, the specification is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: specifying many salts and leaving it to the public to choose, when only one actually works, can render the specification impeachable for insufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: If one of several asserted effects is not produced, specification is bad
rubrics_metrics.description: When several effects are specified and one of them is not produced, the specification is defective and the patent may be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee should not claim results that are not actually achieved by the described invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings must be correct
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorrect drawings make the specification bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings should accurately represent the invention; material errors in figures can contribute to insufficiency or ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a patent claims several distinct things and any one is not new, entire patent may be void
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee applies for a patent reciting improvements in several things and it turns out that one of them lacks novelty, the entire patent may be void because the consideration for the grant fails in part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities (e.g., Brunton v. Hawkes, Hill v. Thompson) suggest the consideration is entire; failure of novelty in any claimed part can invalidate the whole grant unless the patent had been properly limited to a valid part alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee not required to describe rudiments or mere incidents, nor every utensil for known states
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule that new parts must be described does not extend to the rudiments of a science or mere incidents of a subject; known utensils or manners of putting a material into a known state need not be described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: directing that gold be used in fusion does not require describing the utensils or exact manner for fusing gold; only material and novel parts need detailed description.
